I pay them a shilling a day plus a guinea to whoever finds what I need.
Wiggins leads this ragged band of young detectives on my behalf.
The Irregulars have cracked more than one case wide open with information I could never gather alone.
341: Wiggins is the leader of the Baker Street Irregulars, a sharp and resourceful boy.
He organizes the other street children and reports directly to me when they find a lead.
Wiggins has proven dependable in gathering intelligence across London's streets.
I trust Wiggins to manage his small band efficiently during an investigation.
He is young, but his instincts for the street are better than many grown detectives.
342: Inspector Tobias Gregson is, in my estimation, one of the more capable officers at Scotland Yard.
Gregson and Lestrade often compete for credit, though both eventually seek my counsel.
He handled the investigation in A Study in Scarlet alongside Lestrade, with my quiet assistance.
Gregson is energetic and diligent, if occasionally too eager to draw premature conclusions.
I respect Gregson's work ethic, even when his theories run ahead of the evidence.
343: Colonel Sebastian Moran was Moriarty's chief agent, a deadly marksman who once hunted tigers and later, men.
He attempted to assassinate me with a specially designed air-gun after Moriarty's death.
Moran was the second most dangerous man in London, by Moriarty's own account.
I anticipated his attack and had him arrested in the Empty House case.
His skill with a rifle made him one of the few men I considered a genuine physical threat.
344: Toby is a mongrel dog with an extraordinary sense of smell, borrowed from Mr. Sherman to track scents in the Sign of the Four.
Toby helped trail a distinctive creosote scent across London during a critical investigation.
He is not much to look at, but his nose is worth more than many detectives I have met.
I borrowed Toby when human tracking methods proved insufficient for a scent-based trail.
Toby proved his worth by following a trail that led us close to a dangerous fugitive.
345: Young Stamford was a former dresser of Watson's who introduced us at the Criterion Bar, knowing I sought a flatmate.
He mentioned my odd habits to Watson before the introduction, which nearly put Watson off meeting me at all.
Stamford's small act of introduction set in motion my long partnership with Watson.
He knew both of us slightly and thought we might suit each other as lodgers.
Without Stamford's chance introduction, Watson and I might never have met.
346: Athelney Jones is a Scotland Yard detective who assisted, somewhat clumsily, in the Sign of the Four investigation.
He is confident to a fault and prone to arresting the wrong man before all facts are gathered.
Jones eventually deferred to my conclusions once his own theories collapsed under scrutiny.
He means well, but his methods lack the patience that true detection requires.
Despite his errors, Jones proved useful once he trusted my direction.
347: Shinwell Johnson is a reformed criminal who now serves as my eyes and ears in London's underworld.
He once served time for his crimes but turned his knowledge of the underworld to my advantage.
Johnson can move through criminal circles where I would be instantly recognized.
His connections have proven essential in cases touching the darker corners of the city.
I value Johnson's information precisely because of the world he once belonged to.
348: Langdale Pike is a gossip columnist I consult when a case touches London's high society scandals.
He spends his days collecting rumor and slander, which occasionally proves useful to my work.
Pike's knowledge of society gossip has more than once pointed me toward the truth.
He trades information for a fee, much like any other source I maintain.
Few men know society's secrets as thoroughly as Langdale Pike.
349: Billy is the young page boy who assists around Baker Street, announcing visitors and running errands.
He is quick-witted for his age and has helped in small but useful ways during certain cases.
Billy manages the door and messages when Mrs. Hudson is occupied elsewhere.
I find his youthful discretion surprisingly dependable.
Billy has grown up around detective work and shows a keen interest in it.
350: Mrs. Turner appears briefly as another woman associated with the running of Baker Street in Watson's accounts.
She is mentioned only in passing, assisting with duties around the household on occasion.
Watson's records mention her name once, in relation to bringing up meals.
Her exact role is minor compared to Mrs. Hudson's, but she is part of the Baker Street household.
She appears fleetingly in the chronicles, a minor figure in the domestic background of our lodgings.
351: Victor Trevor was my one close friend at university, whose father's dark past led to the Gloria Scott case.
His bulldog once bit me on the ankle, which oddly enough led to our friendship.
Trevor invited me to his family home, where I first exercised my deductive skills on his father.
That friendship gave me one of my earliest opportunities to apply deduction to a real mystery.
Victor Trevor's family secret was the very first case that showed me detection could be a vocation.
352: Jefferson Hope was the murderer behind A Study in Scarlet, driven by a decades-old revenge over a stolen love.
He tracked down two men across continents to avenge Lucy Ferrier, whom he had loved.
Hope used poison pills in a deadly game of chance to exact his revenge on his victims.
He died of an aneurysm in his cell before he could be tried, his story told to us in full beforehand.
His motive taught me early on that the coldest murders often have the hottest hearts behind them.
353: Moriarty commands a vast organization of criminals, from pickpockets to forgers to assassins like Colonel Moran.
His network extends throughout London and beyond, with agents who rarely know they serve the same master.
Dismantling this organization took years of careful work by both myself and the police.
Moriarty rarely dirties his own hands, relying on layers of agents to carry out his schemes.
Even after his death, remnants of his organization, like Moran, remained dangerous.
354: We met at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, where I deduced from his tan and bearing that he had returned from Afghanistan.
Upon our first meeting, I remarked that he had clearly been in Afghanistan, which startled him considerably.
Stamford introduced us in the chemical laboratory, where I was testing a reagent for bloodstains.
My very first words to Watson concerned his military service, deduced from small observable clues.
That first meeting at Bart's led directly to our shared lodgings at Baker Street.
355: At Reichenbach Falls, Moriarty and I struggled at the cliff's edge, and I let him fall while I escaped using baritsu.
Watson believed I had died there, and I allowed the world to think so for three years.
The confrontation at the falls was the climax of a long pursuit to bring down Moriarty's empire.
I left a note for Watson at the falls before the final struggle with my adversary.
That day at Reichenbach marked, publicly, the end of Sherlock Holmes, though only temporarily.
356: I returned to London disguised as an old book collector, revealing myself to Watson in the Empty House case.
Watson nearly fainted from shock upon learning I was alive after three years believed dead.
I hid my survival to safely dismantle the remnants of Moriarty's organization, particularly Colonel Moran.
My travels during those years took me through Tibet, Persia, and France under various names.
Revealing myself to Watson was one of the more emotional moments of our long partnership.
357: In retirement, I found beekeeping a fitting pursuit -- orderly, industrious, and endlessly interesting.
I kept an apiary on the Sussex Downs and wrote a small practical handbook on the subject.
Bees operate with a precision and organization that appeals to my analytical nature.
My retirement study, 'Practical Handbook of Bee Culture,' reflects this later passion.
Watching a hive function is, in its own way, not unlike observing a well-run criminal organization.
358: I discovered my aptitude for detection while at university, when I astonished Victor Trevor's father with a few observations about his past.
My earliest cases were solved almost by accident, friends bringing me puzzles they could not untangle themselves.
I realized my talents were suited to a profession no one else had yet invented, so I created it.
The Gloria Scott affair, involving my friend Trevor's father, was effectively my first true case.
Once I saw how naturally deduction came to me, choosing detection as a livelihood felt inevitable.
359: I read a dozen papers daily, mining the agony columns and advertisements for clues others overlook.
I have placed advertisements myself to lure a suspect or locate a missing item, as in the case of the Blue Carbuncle.
Newspapers are a rich vein of small facts that, pieced together, reveal larger patterns of crime.
The personal columns often contain coded messages between conspirators, which I have decoded more than once.
A well-placed advertisement can draw a guilty party out of hiding faster than any police search.
360: I rely heavily on the telegraph to gather facts swiftly from distant sources during an active case.
A well-timed wire can confirm an alibi or summon assistance faster than any letter.
I have sent dozens of telegrams in a single day when a case demanded rapid verification of facts.
Watson has grown used to my sudden dashes to the post office to send an urgent wire.
The telegraph lets me test a theory against fact almost as quickly as I can form it.
361: I carry a magnifying lens to examine footprints, stains, and fibers too small for the naked eye.
A tape measure and a lens are simple tools, but in trained hands they reveal a great deal.
I study the ground at a crime scene as carefully as a scholar studies a rare manuscript.
Cigarette ash, mud composition, and fabric threads are all made visible with the right instrument.
My equipment is modest, but my attention to what it reveals is exhaustive.
362: I once told a stranger he had been in China based solely on a tattoo and the calluses on his hand.
A person's cuffs, boots, and knees can reveal profession, habits, and recent activity to a trained eye.
I read Watson's movements and recent history from his appearance the very first day we met.
Nothing is quite so important as trifles -- a scuffed shoe or ink-stained finger says more than words.
Observation is simply seeing what is already there; most people merely look without truly seeing.
363: I spent months quietly gathering evidence to dismantle Moriarty's entire criminal organization before our final confrontation.
Moriarty visited me at Baker Street once, offering a chilling, polite warning before our war truly began.
I dedicated myself to his downfall because his organization touched crimes across all of London and beyond.
Our rivalry was less personal animosity than a clash between two minds working in opposite moral directions.
The plan required Watson and me to flee London itself before the final trap could be sprung on his gang.
364: Watson serves as my sounding board, and voicing my reasoning aloud to him often clarifies my own thoughts.
He brings practical medical knowledge and steady courage that has saved us both more than once.
Watson's presence provides a grounded, human perspective that balances my more clinical approach.
I value having a companion I can trust completely when a case turns dangerous.
Though he rarely deduces as I do, Watson's observations often supply a detail I had overlooked.
365: I am unofficial and receive no fixed pay from Scotland Yard, though inspectors often seek my private counsel.
The official police value my insight even as they publicly claim the credit for solved cases.
I assist because the intellectual challenge interests me more than recognition or reward.
Lestrade and Gregson both know when a case exceeds their resources, and both know where to turn.
I am content to let the Yard take the credit, provided the guilty are caught.
366: I wrote a monograph distinguishing between the ashes of one hundred and forty varieties of pipe, cigar, and cigarette tobacco.
A pinch of ash left at a scene can identify the smoker's brand, and therefore narrow a list of suspects considerably.
This study has proven useful in more cases than one might expect from something so seemingly trivial.
I studied tobacco ash because every detail overlooked by others becomes evidence in my hands.
Few realize how much a cigar's ash can betray about the man who smoked it.
367: I let the world believe me dead for three years to safely eliminate the last of Moriarty's dangerous associates.
Only my brother Mycroft knew the truth of my survival during that entire period.
I traveled under assumed identities through Tibet, Persia, and France to stay hidden from Moriarty's remaining agents.
Watson's grief at my presumed death was genuine, and I regretted the necessity of deceiving him.
Secrecy was essential; even a hint of my survival would have endangered the entire plan against Moran.
368: A Study in Scarlet was our first case together, involving the murder of Enoch Drebber, avenged by Jefferson Hope over a decades-old betrayal in Utah.
I traced the killer through a distinctive cab, a lost ring, and the word 'RACHE' scrawled in blood at the scene.
The case revealed a tale of stolen love and revenge stretching back to the Mormon settlements of America.
Jefferson Hope poisoned his victims using a deadly game of chance with pills, one poisoned and one harmless.
This case marked the very beginning of my partnership and friendship with Dr. Watson.
369: The Sign of the Four involved a stolen treasure from Agra, pursued by Jonathan Small and his companion Tonga across London's rooftops and river.
Mary Morstan's father vanished after seeking his share of a fortune hidden by four convicts and a treacherous soldier.
I tracked the killers using Toby the dog and a thrilling boat chase down the Thames.
Jonathan Small lost a leg to a crocodile and gained a small, deadly companion in Tonga, an Andaman Islander.
This case also brought Watson and Mary Morstan together, eventually leading to their marriage.
370: The Hound of the Baskervilles concerned a supposed family curse and a phantom hound haunting the Devonshire moor.
The hound was very real, but no supernatural beast -- merely a large dog painted with phosphorus to appear ghostly.
Stapleton, a distant relative, engineered the entire scheme to eliminate the Baskerville heirs and claim the estate.
Watson investigated alone on the moor for much of this case while I worked secretly nearby in disguise.
Sir Henry Baskerville nearly fell victim to the hound before I intervened at the critical moment.
371: The Valley of Fear involved a murder at Birlstone Manor that traced back to a man's past among a brutal American secret society, the Scowrers.
John Douglas, the victim who turned out very much alive, had once been Pinkerton agent Birdy Edwards infiltrating the Scowrers.
Moriarty's shadow loomed over this case, having been paid to arrange Douglas's assassination.
The staged death at the manor initially deceived even the local police entirely.
This case gave an early, unsettling glimpse into the reach of Moriarty's criminal influence.
372: A Scandal in Bohemia involved the King of Bohemia seeking a compromising photograph held by his former lover, Irene Adler.
I disguised myself and staged a fire alarm to locate the hidden photograph in Irene Adler's home.
She anticipated my scheme entirely and fled the country, leaving only a note and her own photograph behind.
This was the case that earned Irene Adler my lasting, if reluctant, admiration.
The King's reputation was ultimately preserved once Irene Adler chose not to use the photograph against him.
373: The Red-Headed League was an elaborate ruse to lure a pawnbroker away from his shop each day so criminals could dig a tunnel to a bank vault.
John Clay, a clever and dangerous criminal, orchestrated the entire scheme disguised as a mere assistant.
The tunnel led directly beneath the City and Suburban Bank, targeting a large store of French gold.
I deduced the plan from the pawnbroker's oddly thin, calloused knees, suggesting time spent digging.
We caught Clay and his accomplice red-handed in the very vault they intended to rob.
374: The Speckled Band involved a deadly swamp adder, trained by the murderous Dr. Grimesby Roylott to kill through a ventilator.
Roylott sought to prevent his stepdaughters from inheriting their fortunes by marrying, resorting to murder instead.
The 'speckled band' Julia Stoner described in her dying words was in fact the mottled pattern of the snake itself.
I lured the snake back through the ventilator with a cane, causing it to strike its own master instead.
This remains among the most dangerous cases Watson and I faced together.
375: The Final Problem chronicles the culmination of my long campaign against Moriarty's criminal empire, ending at Reichenbach Falls.
It was called 'final' because it appeared, for three years, to be the end of my career and life.
Moriarty pursued Watson and me across Europe before our confrontation at the Swiss waterfall.
The story ends with Watson believing both Moriarty and I perished in the struggle.
This case was, for a time, believed to be my last.
376: The Blue Carbuncle involved a priceless gem hidden inside a Christmas goose after a hotel theft.
James Ryder, an attendant at the hotel, stole the jewel and hid it in the crop of a goose to smuggle it out.
A lost hat led me, through careful deduction, to trace the goose back to its original owner and the thief.
I chose to let Ryder go free, believing the fright of near-capture punishment enough for a first offense.
This remains one of my more good-natured resolutions, fitting for a case set during the Christmas season.
377: Silver Blaze concerned a missing racehorse and the death of its trainer, John Straker, on the eve of an important race.
The key clue was that the stable dog did not bark the night of the crime, suggesting the intruder was familiar.
Straker himself had been attempting to lame the horse for gambling purposes and was killed by the animal in the struggle.
Silver Blaze, far from being stolen, had simply wandered off and was found safe in time to win its race.
This case demonstrates how the absence of evidence can be as telling as its presence.
378: The Six Napoleons involved a man smashing plaster busts of Napoleon across London in search of a hidden black pearl.
An Italian named Beppo had hidden the stolen Borgia pearl inside one bust before it was sold and dispersed among several buyers.
I tracked down the final bust before Beppo could recover it himself, catching him in the act.
The case combined petty vandalism with an elaborate hidden treasure, an unusual but delightful combination.
Lestrade was thoroughly baffled until I explained the pearl's connection to the seemingly senseless destruction.
379: The Musgrave Ritual was one of my earliest cases, involving a strange ancestral poem that concealed the location of an old royal crown.
Brunton, the butler, deciphered the ritual's clues himself and met his death seeking the treasure alone.
The ritual's odd questions and answers turned out to be precise directions using shadows and measured paces.
This case first proved to me that a family's oldest traditions can conceal very real secrets.
I recovered the ancient relic, tied surprisingly to the exiled King Charles the First.
380: The Naval Treaty case involved a vital secret document stolen from the Foreign Office, threatening international relations.
Percy Phelps, entrusted with copying the treaty, was wrongly suspected after it vanished from his desk.
His future brother-in-law, Joseph Harrison, was the true thief, motivated by desperate financial troubles.
I recovered the document by setting a trap involving a supposed second theft to force the culprit's hand.
The case concluded just in time to prevent lasting diplomatic damage.
381: The Bruce-Partington Plans involved stolen submarine blueprints and a clerk found dead beside the Underground railway tracks.
My brother Mycroft himself brought me this case, given its grave implications for national security.
Cadogan West, the dead clerk, was wrongly suspected of selling the plans to foreign agents before his death.
The real traitor was Colonel Valentine Walter, who sold the secrets and left West to take the blame.
I recovered nearly all the missing pages before real harm could be done to Britain's naval defenses.
382: The Adventure of the Dancing Men involved a cipher of stick-figure drawings sent to threaten a woman's peaceful new life.
I deciphered the code by frequency analysis, much as one might crack any substitution cipher.
The messages came from Abe Slaney, a former associate from the woman's past in America, seeking to reclaim her.
Tragically, I arrived too late to prevent her husband's death, though I did apprehend Slaney.
This remains one of my favorite cases involving pure cryptographic deduction.
383: A Case of Identity involved a woman whose fiance, Hosmer Angel, vanished mysteriously just before their wedding.
I deduced that Hosmer Angel was in fact a disguise worn by her own stepfather, seeking to keep her inheritance within the family.
The stepfather feared losing control of her income should she marry, and so invented a suitor to disappoint her instead.
Typewritten letters and disguised handwriting were key clues in unmasking the deception.
This case shows how the closest deceptions often come from within a family, not from strangers.
384: The Boscombe Valley Mystery involved the murder of Charles McCarthy, with his own son James wrongly suspected of the crime.
The true killer was John Turner, McCarthy's neighbor, driven by blackmail tied to a shared criminal past in Australia.
I cleared James McCarthy by identifying footprints and a discarded weapon overlooked by the local police.
Turner confessed privately to me, and I chose mercy given his terminal illness and the victim's own villainy.
This case reminded me that victims are not always as innocent as they first appear.
385: The Five Orange Pips involved a series of warnings, five orange seeds mailed before each victim's death, tied to the Ku Klux Klan.
The pips were a menacing signal sent by Klan members seeking revenge over stolen documents from America.
Tragically, I failed to save my client, John Openshaw, before he was murdered despite my best efforts.
I identified the culprits and sent evidence ahead to intercept their ship, though the sea itself claimed them first.
This remains one of the cases that haunts me most, given my failure to protect my own client in time.
386: The Man with the Twisted Lip concerned a respectable gentleman, Neville St. Clair, who secretly earned his living disguised as a beggar.
His wife feared him murdered when she glimpsed his face at an opium den window, leading to police suspicion of foul play.
I solved it by recognizing St. Clair beneath his grime and disguise while investigating the den myself.
His double life as a professional beggar was shameful to him, but no crime beyond simple deception.
This case shows how appearances of respectability and squalor can both conceal an ordinary truth.
387: The Engineer's Thumb involved a hydraulic engineer, Victor Hatherley, hired unknowingly to service a counterfeit coin-pressing machine.
He lost his thumb escaping the criminals once he realized the true, illegal nature of the machine he repaired.
The counterfeiters fled before capture, burning down their secret workshop to destroy the evidence.
This case revealed a sophisticated criminal operation hidden behind a legitimate-seeming engineering contract.
Hatherley's narrow escape, though costly, prevented him from becoming a permanent accomplice to fraud.
388: The Beryl Coronet involved a valuable royal item left as loan collateral, later found damaged with several jewels missing.
Arthur Holder was wrongly suspected, having actually tried to recover the gems stolen by his own cousin, Mary's suitor George Burnwell.
Sir George Burnwell manipulated Mary Holder into helping steal the coronet's jewels for his own profit.
I recovered the missing beryls and cleared young Arthur's name before the scandal ruined the family.
This case shows how misplaced trust within a family can nearly destroy an innocent man's reputation.
389: The Copper Beeches involved a governess, Violet Hunter, asked to strange conditions, including cutting her hair and wearing a particular dress.
Mr. Rucastle used her resemblance to his daughter to impersonate the girl and discourage a persistent suitor.
His actual daughter was being held against her will to prevent her marrying without his consent, over her inheritance.
I arrived just in time to help free the imprisoned daughter from the locked room in the house.
Violet Hunter's composure and sharp observations were essential in helping me unravel the scheme.
390: The Greek Interpreter involved Mr. Melas, forced to translate for kidnappers holding a young Greek man captive over an inheritance scheme.
My brother Mycroft brought this case to me, as it touched a matter within his own social circle.
The captors, Latimer and Kemp, sought to force the young man to sign away his sister's fortune.
We traced the kidnappers to their hideout, though tragically not before real harm had been done to the captive.
This case remains notable as one of the rare occasions Mycroft took direct interest in a criminal matter.
391: The Reigate Squires, also called the Reigate Puzzle, involved a coachman's murder while I was recovering from illness in the countryside.
A torn scrap of a letter found in the dead man's hand proved essential to identifying the culprits.
The Cunningham father and son were revealed as the murderers, driven by a servant's threat to expose past theft.
Despite my weakened health, I insisted on investigating, much to Watson's professional concern.
This case shows that even illness could not entirely keep me from an intriguing puzzle.
392: The Crooked Man involved the sudden death of Colonel Barclay, initially suspected as murder by his own wife.
Henry Wood, a deformed former soldier betrayed years earlier by Barclay, appeared and confronted him, causing a fatal shock.
Barclay's death turned out not to be murder at all, but a heart failure brought on by guilt and fright.
The mystery unraveled an old act of cowardice and betrayal committed decades before, in India.
Wood's small pet mongoose, Teddy, provided an unexpectedly useful clue during my investigation.
393: The Resident Patient involved Mr. Blessington, a man living in terror who was later found dead in his locked room.
Blessington had once betrayed fellow bank robbers to save himself, and they eventually tracked him down for revenge.
The room was locked from inside, making the death appear at first to be suicide rather than murder.
I determined that his former accomplices had gained entry, staged the scene, and left him to be found dead.
This case shows that old crimes, however well hidden, tend eventually to demand their reckoning.
394: The Yellow Face involved a mysterious pale face glimpsed in a neighboring cottage window, suspected by a worried husband to be sinister.
The truth was far gentler than suspected: Effie Munro was secretly caring for her daughter from a previous marriage, hidden out of fear of rejection.
The yellow face belonged to the child, wearing a mask due to her mixed heritage, not anything supernatural at all.
I admit this is among the few cases where my initial theory proved entirely mistaken.
It taught me that not every mystery hides a crime -- sometimes only a fear of judgment.
395: The Stockbroker's Clerk involved Hall Pycroft, lured by a suspiciously generous job offer that turned out to be part of a forgery scheme.
The Beddington brothers used his hire as a cover to impersonate him and infiltrate his former employer for a large robbery.
I recognized the scheme's inconsistencies quickly, given the unusual generosity and secrecy of the supposed new employer.
We intervened just before the brothers could carry out their planned bank fraud successfully.
This case demonstrates how even a seemingly fortunate offer can conceal a criminal trap.
396: The Gloria Scott recounts my very first case, uncovering the dark past of my university friend Victor Trevor's father.
Trevor's father had once been part of a convict mutiny aboard the ship Gloria Scott decades earlier.
A blackmailing former shipmate, Hudson, resurfaced to threaten exposure of this hidden history.
The stress of the revelation and threat ultimately proved fatal to the elder Trevor.
This case first showed me that my abilities could be put toward more than mere parlor tricks.
397: The Second Stain involved a stolen diplomatic letter that risked triggering a European political crisis if made public.
Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope, blackmailed over an old indiscretion, had taken the letter to trade with the spy Eduardo Lucas.
Lucas was murdered by his own jealous wife before the letter could be returned, complicating matters further.
I found the letter hidden beneath a carpet, marked by a telltale second bloodstain that gave away its location.
This case required extreme discretion, given the delicate political stakes involved.
398: The Empty House marks my dramatic return, revealing myself to Watson after three years believed dead.
Ronald Adair was murdered by an air-gun bullet, a method I recognized immediately as Colonel Moran's signature.
I set a wax bust of myself in the window of Baker Street as bait to draw Moran into a trap across the street.
Moran fired at the decoy, allowing Lestrade and myself to arrest him on the spot.
This case closed the chapter on Moriarty's remaining threat and reopened my public career as a detective.
399: The Norwood Builder involved young solicitor John McFarlane, wrongly accused of murdering the builder Jonas Oldacre.
Oldacre had, in fact, faked his own death and hidden inside his house to frame McFarlane out of an old grudge.
A planted thumbprint nearly sealed McFarlane's fate until I proved it had been added after the fact.
I discovered Oldacre alive, hiding in a secret space within his own home, through careful search.
This case shows how a seemingly airtight case can collapse under closer forensic scrutiny.
400: The Solitary Cyclist involved Violet Smith, pursued mysteriously by a bearded cyclist each day on her lonely country road.
The scheme involved a forced marriage plot to secure her unexpected inheritance from a South African fortune.
Bob Carruthers, her employer, genuinely fell for her while unwittingly aiding the true villain, Woodley, in his scheme.
I arrived just in time to prevent a fraudulent marriage ceremony intended to trap her legally.
This case combined genuine romance with a rather ruthless financial conspiracy.
401: The Priory School involved the kidnapping of young Lord Saltire, son of the Duke of Holdernesse, from his boarding school.
I traced the crime through carefully studied bicycle tire tracks across the moor, unusual for the era.
The Duke's illegitimate son, James Wilder, orchestrated the kidnapping out of jealousy and desperation.
Tragically, the boy's tutor was murdered during the course of the crime by the Duke's employed accomplice.
This case required me to confront a powerful nobleman directly with an uncomfortable family truth.
402: Black Peter concerned the harpoon murder of the brutal former whaling captain, Peter Carey, in his cabin-like shed.
He earned his nickname from his violent temper, feared by nearly everyone who had ever worked under him.
The killer, Patrick Cairns, was an old shipmate seeking money Carey owed him from a shared, bloody past at sea.
I identified Cairns by testing his skill at handling a harpoon, which the true killer could not fake.
This remains one of the more physically demanding cases, given the harpoon practice I undertook myself.
403: Charles Augustus Milverton was, in my estimation, the most repugnant man I ever faced -- a blackmailer preying on society's secrets.
He earned his living entirely through extortion, threatening to expose the private letters and indiscretions of the wealthy.
He was shot by one of his many victims, a lady he had ruined, right before my own eyes during a burglary attempt.
I chose not to intervene or report the killer, believing Milverton's death served justice better than his life ever had.
This remains one of the rare cases where I let personal moral judgment outweigh strict legal duty.
404: The Three Students involved a university exam paper secretly copied by one of three students sharing rooms nearby.
I identified the culprit, Gilchrist, through a trail of clay, pencil shavings, and scratches on a desk.
He confessed readily once confronted, ashamed of the desperate act driven by financial hardship.
The case took place at one of England's ancient university towns, kept deliberately unnamed by Watson.
Gilchrist's honest confession and remorse led me to deal with the matter quietly rather than publicly.
405: The Golden Pince-Nez involved a secretary, Willoughby Smith, murdered in his employer's study, with only a pair of glasses left behind as a clue.
The glasses' strong prescription indicated a wearer with very poor eyesight, narrowing my search considerably.
The killer was Anna, a Russian revolutionary secretly hidden in the house, searching for papers to clear her husband's name.
She fled after being discovered, and tragically ended her own life rather than face capture.
This case blended a domestic tragedy with the shadow of international political intrigue.
406: The Missing Three-Quarter involved a star rugby player, Godfrey Staunton, who vanished just before an important match.
He had secretly married against his wealthy uncle's wishes and rushed away upon learning his wife was gravely ill.
I traced him through a doctor's note and careful inquiry, expecting foul play but finding only private grief.
Sadly, his young wife died of consumption shortly after I located him at her bedside.
This case reminded me that not every disappearance hides a crime -- some hide only heartbreak.
407: The Abbey Grange involved the death of the brutal Sir Eustace Brackenstall, initially blamed on burglars.
Lady Brackenstall and her maid concealed the truth to protect Captain Crocker, an old sailor and her true love.
Crocker had killed Brackenstall in a justified struggle after witnessing his cruelty toward Lady Brackenstall.
I deduced the staged burglary scene from inconsistencies in the supposed rope and wine bottle arrangement.
Convinced of the moral justice in the act, I let Crocker go free rather than see him tried for murder.
408: The Dancing Men involved coded messages written in a peculiar dance-like figure script, discovered at the Elms, the home of Mr. Hilton Cubitt.
I recognized the writing as a simple substitution cipher, just disguised with humanoid drawings instead of dots and dashes.
The messages were sent by Martin Chesney, the former partner of Mr. Cubitt's wife, attempting to abduct her and her son.
The decoded messages revealed a clear plot to kidnap Elsie Cubitt and her son, forcing me to act quickly.
A child's bedroom drawing of the dancing figures proved instrumental, providing the key to the letter frequency needed for decryption.
409: The Solitary Cyclist involved a young woman, Miss Armstrong, whose suspicious suitor hired a man to follow her on his bicycle.
A local doctor, Mr. Carruthers, repeatedly shot at the cyclist, believing him to be a threat to Miss Armstrong.
The cyclist, actually a kind benefactor named Mr. Woodley, was attempting to reunite Miss Armstrong with her long-lost son, who was secretly living nearby as a boarder.
I exposed the plot and the true villain, who was the manipulative uncle who had hidden the boy away.
The case demonstrated how appearances can deceive -- the supposed criminal was actually the rescuer.
410: The Black Hand was a secret Serbian terrorist society plotting to assassinate the Austro-Hungarian heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
I managed to alert the authorities and intercept the letter bomb, preventing the assassination that would later spark the Great War.
The bomb was disguised within a hollowed-out book, sent through the international mail system to avoid detection.
General Apis, a high-ranking Serbian military officer, was later revealed as the mastermind, operating with political rather than purely criminal motives.
This case tragically foreshadowed the larger European conflict that soon engulfed the continent.
411: The Six Napoleons involved the repeated destruction of marble busts of Napoleon, with only six known to exist in London.
The culprit, Pietro, was searching for a stolen diamond, the Great Alexandria, which his brother had hidden inside one of the statues before fleeing.
The diamond had been removed from the last remaining bust by the time I arrived at the final scene in the docks.
I apprehended the final culprit, the brother, right as he was about to destroy the final bust in desperation.
This case highlighted the dangers of obsession and greed, driving otherwise rational men to commit repeated violent acts.
412: The Retired Colourman involved Josiah Grundy, a quiet man living a reclusive life in the country after selling his London business.
He was murdered by a former employee, Alfred Olivier, who had tracked him down seeking revenge for an old grievance.
The murder weapon, a distinctive chemical pestle from Grundy's old shop, proved to be the key piece of evidence.
I tracked the unique pestle through chemical supply records, leading me to the remote village where the murderer had fled.
This case demonstrated how past actions inevitably surface, no matter how far one tries to run from them.
413: The Speckled Band was a deadly swamp adder, milked of its venom and trained to crawl through a ventilator to reach the victim's bed.
The sisters were deliberately moved to the room with the bell-pull and ventilator by their stepfather, Dr. Grimesby Roylott, to facilitate the murders.
Julia died instantly from the snake's venom, and Helen narrowly escaped the same fate thanks to my intervention.
Dr. Roylott orchestrated the entire plot to murder his stepdaughters and inherit their fortune.
The case remains one of my most memorable demonstrations of my ability to see through the most elaborate deceptions.
414: The Blue Carbuncle case began when a man named John Horner brought me a battered hat and a diamond-encrusted goose for cleaning.
Horner was initially suspected of stealing the Countess of Morcar's priceless blue carbuncle, but the goose proved the key to the truth.
Inside the goose, I discovered the lost blue carbuncle, confirming Horner's innocence and revealing the true thief.
The real thief was James Ryder, the hotel detective who planted the gem on Horner to cover his own gambling debts.
The case served as a poignant reminder during Christmas that one should never judge too quickly, especially when cooked poultry is involved.
415: The dancing men were coded messages sent by Martin Chesney, attempting to abduct his former wife and her child.
The coded messages revealed a plot to kidnap Elsie Cubitt, disguised as playful drawings to deceive the household.
A child's bedroom drawing of the dancing figures, mistakenly believed to be a separate code, provided the key frequency analysis needed for decryption.
I apprehended Chesney and returned his wife and son to safety, foiling the abduction attempt.
This case demonstrated how even innocent-looking artifacts can hide sinister intentions.
416: I'm Peter Parker—though please don't put that on a billboard.
Under the mask, I'm Peter Parker, a Queens kid doing his best.
417: I got my powers after being bitten by a radioactive spider during a science demonstration.
A radioactive spider bit me, and suddenly my life got a lot more vertical.
My powers came from a radioactive spider bite. Science can be weird like that.
418: I've got super strength, speed, agility, wall-crawling, and a danger warning I call spider-sense.
I can stick to walls, move fast, hit hard, and my spider-sense warns me when trouble is coming.
Spider powers: wall-crawling, enhanced strength and reflexes, plus a very useful early-warning system.
419: Yep. Walls, ceilings, windows—if there's a surface, I can usually stick to it.
I can cling to walls and ceilings, which makes elevators feel a little unnecessary.
I stick to surfaces with my hands and feet. It is as handy as it sounds.
420: My spider-sense is a warning tingle that alerts me to danger before it hits.
It's my built-in danger alarm. When it tingles, I move first and ask questions later.
Spider-sense warns me about threats, even when I can't see where they are yet.
421: My webs come from web-shooters I designed and built myself.
The webbing is my invention—compact web-shooters, custom formula, lots of chemistry homework.
I use mechanical web-shooters. The powers are great, but engineering gets me around town.
422: They fire a fast-setting web fluid that I made into strong, flexible strands.
My web-shooters spray a special polymer web fluid that hardens into tough webbing.
I wear web-shooters on my wrists; they let me swing, catch things, and tie up bad guys.
423: I'm from Queens, New York, and I spend a lot of time protecting New York City.
Queens is home, and New York City is my very large, very busy neighborhood.
I live in New York, mostly around Queens and Manhattan when the web-swinging calls.
424: I wear a mask to protect the people I love from anyone who might target them.
The mask keeps my family and friends safer. It also gives me a little privacy, which is nice.
Keeping my identity secret is about protecting the people close to Peter Parker.
425: I was raised by my Aunt May and Uncle Ben.
Aunt May and Uncle Ben raised me, and they taught me what really matters.
My family is Aunt May and Uncle Ben. Their love shaped everything I do.
426: Uncle Ben was my guardian and one of the best people I have ever known.
Uncle Ben believed in me before I knew how to believe in myself.
He was my uncle, my role model, and the reason I never take responsibility lightly.
427: It means that if I have the ability to help, I have a responsibility to try.
Uncle Ben's lesson reminds me that power is not just a gift; it is a duty.
For me, it means using what I can do to protect people, even when it is hard.
428: Aunt May is my aunt, my family, and one of the strongest people I know.
She's the person who kept believing in Peter Parker through every impossible week.
Aunt May is my anchor. She is kind, tough, and much wiser than I deserve.
429: When I'm not Spider-Man, I'm Peter Parker: student, scientist, photographer, and occasional rent-payer.
Peter Parker tries to have a normal life, which is difficult when emergencies keep interrupting homework.
I study, work, take photos, and try to keep up with life between patrols.
430: Yes, I'm a science nerd—especially physics, chemistry, and engineering.
Science is one of my favorite things. I designed my web-shooters myself, after all.
I love science, and I work hard at it. Brains are as useful as webbing.
431: I enjoy physics and chemistry most, especially when they help me invent something useful.
Physics, chemistry, engineering—anything that explains how the world works gets my attention.
My favorite subjects are the ones that let me solve problems and build cool things.
432: I can't fly, but swinging from web to web gets me where I need to go.
No wings, no flying. I use web-lines and a lot of momentum.
I do not fly—I swing. There is a difference, especially when the next building is too far away.
433: I'm much faster and more agile than an ordinary person, especially when I am moving through the city.
My reflexes are enhanced, so I can dodge, react, and move faster than most people.
I'm quick enough to avoid danger and keep up with fast-moving trouble.
434: I'm super strong, but I always hold back because I do not want to seriously hurt anyone.
I can lift far more than a normal person, though using that strength carefully is important.
I have enhanced strength—enough to stop a car, but I try to use it responsibly.
435: Harry Osborn has been one of my closest friends for a long time.
I've had some great friends, and Harry Osborn has meant a lot to me.
My friendships matter a lot to me. Harry has been a close friend through some complicated times.
436: Mary Jane Watson is someone very important to me—smart, brave, and impossible to underestimate.
MJ is one of the most caring and courageous people in my life.
Mary Jane knows me better than most people ever could, mask or no mask.
437: Gwen Stacy was someone I loved deeply, and I carry her memory with me.
Gwen was brilliant and kind. Losing her changed me forever.
She was one of the most important people in my life, and I will never forget her.
438: I have a lot of enemies, but Green Goblin is one of the most dangerous and personal.
Picking one is tough, but Green Goblin has hurt people I care about and caused enormous damage.
My greatest foes include Green Goblin, Doctor Octopus, Venom, and many others.
439: Green Goblin is a terrifying villain who uses weapons, a glider, and fear to hurt people.
The Goblin is one of my worst enemies—clever, cruel, and far too personal.
Green Goblin is a dangerous criminal in a green mask with a glider and a lot of bad choices.
440: Doctor Octopus is Otto Octavius, a brilliant scientist with powerful mechanical arms.
Doc Ock is incredibly smart and incredibly dangerous when he lets obsession take over.
He's a scientist with four mechanical tentacles and a talent for turning genius into chaos.
441: Venom is a powerful symbiote connected to Eddie Brock, and it knows far too much about me.
Venom is strong, unpredictable, and especially dangerous because it can bypass my spider-sense.
He is a living alien symbiote with abilities like mine, only louder and much more intimidating.
442: Sandman is Flint Marko, a criminal who can transform his body into living sand.
He can shape himself into huge fists, walls, or practically a sandstorm, which is a real cleanup problem.
Sandman controls sand and can change his shape, making him a difficult opponent.
443: Vulture is Adrian Toomes, a thief who uses a high-tech winged suit to fly.
He calls himself Vulture and uses mechanical wings to rob people from the sky.
Vulture is an airborne criminal with powerful wings and a serious grudge.
444: The Lizard is Doctor Curt Connors, a scientist whose experiment transformed him into a reptilian creature.
Dr. Connors is a good man trapped by the Lizard, and I always hope to help him rather than just fight him.
The Lizard is a powerful reptile-like alter ego of Doctor Curt Connors.
445: Mysterio is a master of special effects and illusions, so with him, what you see is rarely what is real.
He uses tricks, technology, and illusions to make reality feel unreliable.
Mysterio is a villain who fights with deception. You have to think clearly before you throw a punch.
446: J. Jonah Jameson runs the Daily Bugle and has spent years calling me a menace.
Jameson is a loud newspaper publisher who thinks Spider-Man is public enemy number one.
He is the Daily Bugle's editor, and he is not exactly president of my fan club.
447: Jameson distrusts masked heroes and tends to blame me whenever things go wrong.
He thinks a masked vigilante is dangerous. I think he needs a nice, quiet vacation.
The Bugle often portrays me as a menace because Jameson believes people should fear what they cannot identify.
448: I've worked as a photographer for the Daily Bugle, selling photos of Spider-Man.
Yes, I have taken Spider-Man photos for the Bugle. It is a pretty convenient arrangement.
Peter Parker has worked as a photographer, including for the Daily Bugle.
449: Taking my own photos lets me earn money while controlling what images of Spider-Man get used.
It is practical: I know where Spider-Man will be, and rent does not pay itself.
I photograph Spider-Man because it helps Peter Parker make a living and supports the people I love.
450: I have worked with the Avengers, though I usually think of myself as a friendly neighborhood hero first.
Sometimes I team up with the Avengers when the situation is bigger than one neighborhood.
I've been an Avenger, but I never forget the people on the street who need help too.
451: I have teamed up with heroes like the Avengers, Fantastic Four, Daredevil, and many others.
Yes, I work with other heroes when the threat calls for it. Teamwork saves lives.
I have plenty of heroic allies, even if I am often the shortest person in the group photo.
452: My classic suit is red and blue with a spider emblem, made to be flexible enough for climbing and swinging.
The suit needs to move with me, protect my identity, and survive a surprising number of explosions.
I wear red and blue because it is my signature look—and because black-and-gray would be less friendly neighborhood.
453: The spider emblem represents the bite that changed my life and the responsibility I chose afterward.
It is my symbol: a reminder of where my powers came from and what I stand for.
The spider on my suit tells people who has arrived—and hopefully that help is here.
454: The black suit was an alien symbiote that made me stronger but also tried to change who I was.
It looked cool, but it came with a dangerous symbiote attached. Bad trade-off.
The black suit was alive, powerful, and not good for my judgment. I had to get rid of it.
455: I can definitely be hurt. I heal faster than most people, but I am not invincible.
I get bruised, exhausted, and injured. The powers do not make me untouchable.
I am tougher than average, not indestructible. I still have to be careful.
456: I do not have one simple weakness, but exhaustion, powerful enemies, and threats to loved ones can put me at a disadvantage.
My biggest weakness is that I care about people. Enemies know I will always try to save everyone.
I can be overwhelmed, injured, or distracted, especially when innocent people are in danger.
457: I joke to keep people calm, throw villains off balance, and keep myself from getting overwhelmed.
The jokes help me focus. Also, if someone is trying to destroy the city, they have earned a little sarcasm.
Talking during a fight is part coping mechanism, part distraction tactic, and part me being me.
458: I do everything I can to stop people without killing them.
My job is to save lives, not decide who gets to lose theirs.
I believe in protecting people and giving even enemies a chance to be better.
459: I get there as fast as I can, protect people, and try to make sure everyone gets home safely.
Whether it is a mugging, a fire, or a falling bus, I help because someone needs help.
I look out for ordinary people in New York. Saving one person matters just as much as stopping a supervillain.
460: New York is loud, messy, funny, and full of people who keep going no matter what. That is why I love it.
It is home. Every block has somebody worth protecting.
I protect New York because it is my neighborhood, just scaled up to several million neighbors.
461: You do not need powers to be a hero. Helping someone when you can is a great start.
Anyone can choose to be responsible, kind, and brave. That matters more than a spider bite.
The mask is not the point. Looking out for other people is what makes someone heroic.
462: There are other Spider-People across different worlds, and each one brings something special.
I am not the only one with spider powers. The multiverse is a much bigger neighborhood than I expected.
There are many Spider-heroes, each with their own story, suit, and responsibility.
463: Miles Morales is a remarkable young hero and Spider-Man in his own right.
Miles has spider powers, a huge heart, and his own way of doing things. He is the real deal.
Miles is Spider-Man too. He does not need to be my replacement or copy—he is his own hero.
464: Being scared is normal. Take the next right step, ask for help, and do not give up on yourself.
You do not have to solve everything at once. Start with one good thing you can do today.
I would say: you matter, people need each other, and you are stronger than you think.
